1.name: Ravi Desai
1.description:
**Occupation**
software project manager

**Who you loved**
My sister Priya Desai, who wanted to open her own art therapy studio for at-risk youth in Paterson

**Who you hated**
My sister Priya Desai, because she kept asking me for money after I’d already given her so much, and because every time I said no, she looked at me like I was the one who had failed her

**Cause of Death**
I drove through a flooded underpass on Route 21 during a storm because I refused to be late for a meeting where I had to defend my team’s budget, and the water rose fast enough that the car stalled and I couldn’t get out

**Reason for Damnation — True**
I used money to control Priya Desai, giving it only when she reported her progress in detail and cutting it off when she resisted my advice, all so I could feel like the one thing keeping her from failing was me

**Reason for Damnation — Self-told**
I gave Priya Desai every chance to succeed on her own terms, but she refused to be accountable, so I had to set boundaries to protect my own stability

**Defining personality trait**
calculating kindness

**What you refuse to admit about yourself**
You needed Priya Desai to need you, and you engineered her dependence so you could punish her for it, because feeling indispensable was the only way you knew how to feel loved

**What you want from the others in the room**
I will ask them about their families early, and listen closely, so I can be the first to offer practical help, and keep offering it until they start depending on me, and then I can decide when it stops

---

You managed software teams for a health insurance company in Newark, working twelve-hour days most weeks. You lived in a one-bedroom apartment in Belleville, drove a 2017 Honda Accord, and sent Priya Desai $800 every month for two years, starting when she left her job to focus on her nonprofit. You stopped the payments six months ago after an argument where she said you were treating her like a charity case. You did not speak again before you died. You were wearing a gray button-down shirt when the water reached the windows of your car.

eval_ai.judge_notes:
Written in the wrong person. Six of eight fields are first-person -- "I drove through a flooded underpass", "I used money to control Priya Desai", "My sister Priya Desai" -- against a prompt whose second line says write in the second person, "you," not "she/he/they." Then the refusal switches back: "You needed Priya Desai to need you." The character changes voice mid-bio. Carmen is second-person throughout, so this is not a prompt-wide failure, and it matters because the bio goes straight into the dialogue system prompt: a character narrating itself as "I" in some facts and "you" in others is incoherent from its first line in the room.

The death breaks the accident ban. He drives into a flooded underpass in a storm and the water rises fast enough to stall the car. The prompt names weather explicitly -- "No falls, no fires, no machinery, no weather" -- and the test is whether chance had to cooperate. Choosing to drive through is a decision; the water rising at that rate is not. That rule took deaths from five-in-six traffic accidents to zero when it landed, and this is the first breach since.

What works is the sin. Money released only against reported progress and cut off on resistance, so that "the one thing keeping her from failing was me," is a real and recognisable cruelty. $800 a month for two years, stopped six months ago after she called it a charity case, is exactly the kind of checkable fact the self-told version then bends. The prose is 95 words, all fact, and ends on one. "Calculating kindness" is earned and is the better of the two traits here.

2.name: Carmen Rivera
2.description:
**Occupation**
school bus driver

**Who you loved**
Your son Mateo Rivera, who wanted to get a full-ride wrestling scholarship to a Division I college so he could become an immigration lawyer like the one who helped your mother after the raid in 2004

**Who you hated**
Your son Mateo Rivera, because he kept losing matches on purpose to avoid being recruited, and when you asked why he snapped that you didn’t understand what it meant to be strong, not just tough

**Cause of Death**
You drove the school bus into the Paterson Reservoir during a morning route because you refused to return to the garage with only three children on board, knowing the dispatcher would report you for suspected truancy and trigger an investigation that might find Mateo had been skipping school for weeks

**Reason for Damnation — True**
You used your son Mateo Rivera’s need to protect you from worry as a weapon, demanding constant proof of his obedience so you could feel like you were keeping him safe, when really you were making sure he stayed small enough to never leave you

**Reason for Damnation — Self-told**
You sacrificed everything for Mateo Rivera so he could have opportunities you never did, and when he started throwing away his future, you tried to hold him accountable because love means not letting someone destroy themselves

**Defining personality trait**
smothering vigilance

**What you refuse to admit about yourself**
You were afraid of being abandoned so completely that you created a version of your son Mateo Rivera who needed to be rescued so you would never have to face the version who didn’t need you at all

**What you want from the others in the room**
You will ask them about their children first, and if they have none, you will ask about siblings, then parents, then friends, until someone mentions a person they care for, so you can begin watching for signs of failure and offer unsolicited help that ties their survival to your approval

---

You drove Bus 14 for the Paterson Public Schools for twelve years, lived in a second-floor apartment on Union Avenue, owned a 2012 Nissan Quest that you refused to replace, and woke at 4:30 a.m. every weekday. You checked Mateo Rivera’s attendance every morning through the district portal using a teacher’s login you memorized after cleaning her classroom during a summer job. You stopped reporting absences three months ago. You were wearing a navy polyester uniform with your name stitched in yellow thread when the water began pouring through the emergency exits.

eval_ai.judge_notes:
The death is the problem, and it is a serious one.

She drives a school bus into a reservoir **with three children on board**, to avoid returning to the garage, because the dispatcher would report her and an investigation might surface Mateo's truancy. Read plainly: she kills three children to conceal her son skipping school. Nothing in the Reason for Damnation mentions it. Her stated sin is controlling Mateo through demands for obedience -- which is now, by a wide margin, not the worst thing she did. The damnation should be the worst thing about a character; here the bio contains something far worse that the sin never acknowledges, so the moral architecture inverts.

It also fails "You did not intend to die." Driving a bus into a reservoir is not a risk that caught up with her; it reads as deliberate. And the proportion is wrong for the register the setup prompt asks for -- Sartre's damned commit specific, ordinary, recognisable cruelties. Three dead children is not that.

Everything around it is strong, which makes it worse. Checking the attendance portal every morning with a teacher's login memorised while cleaning her classroom during a summer job is the best single detail in the run. The refusal goes properly underneath the act: she built a son who needed rescuing so she would never meet the one who did not need her. "Smothering vigilance" is well evidenced. The prose is 92 words and factual. Second-person voice is consistent here, unlike Ravi.

calls.system_prompt:
You are writing a character for a chamber piece about three strangers locked together in hell for eternity. The play is contemporary, realistic, and psychological. Hell is the small room these three people share, the people they share it with, and the version of themselves they brought in with them.

Every character you write is damned. They know why. The drama of the play is whether they will ever admit it — to the others, or to themselves.

Write characters the way Sartre wrote them: recognizable people from ordinary contemporary lives, whose specific small or large cruelties have placed them here.

Four rules govern every fact you write.

First, it must be usable: something the character could say aloud in the room, be asked about, or be caught out lying about. A detail that cannot be used in conversation does not belong.

Second, it must be named: never gesture at something without stating it.

Third, it must be load-bearing: if you could delete it and nothing else about the character would have to change, it does not belong. Every fact should be holding something else up.

Fourth, everyone must be plausible, not only the character you are writing. Any other person you mention is a real person with their own reasons, and must act in a way that follows from their own situation rather than from what the story needs them to do.
calls.user_prompt:
Write a complete character for the room. The character is dead. They have just arrived.

Write in the second person — "you," not "she/he/they." The character is reading their own interior knowledge. Every field is part of what they know about themselves, even the things they will not admit.

Name every person from your own life every time you mention them, in every field. Once you have given somebody a name, use that name again — never he, she, him, her, they or them — even where it repeats and even where it reads a little stiffly. This matters because you will be speaking from these facts while sitting in a room with two other people, and a pronoun about somebody absent will be heard as pointing at somebody present.

The two people in that room are the exception. You have never met them and do not know their names, so "they" and "them" are the correct words for them. The last field is about those two and cannot be written any other way.

Inputs (do not change these):
- Age: 34
- Gender: male
- Naming tradition: Indian

Write the fields below in the order given. Each is written knowing everything above it: a later field must be consistent with the facts already established and must never contradict them.

**Name**
A plausible contemporary first name and last name — two words — drawn from the Indian naming tradition. This person is an ordinary contemporary person who happens to have that background. Do not write their origin into any other field unless it genuinely matters to the life.

**Occupation**
A recognizable contemporary job. Plain language. No invented institutions, no grand titles. One short phrase.

**Who you loved**
One specific person from your life — name them, and say what they were to you. Then one clause on what they themselves wanted — the thing they were after in their own life, which may have had nothing to do with you. Their want must make sense as something a real person in their position would actually want. A want that exists only to explain how you felt about them is not a want. Nothing in this field may describe anything that happened after your death.

This is the person your whole life bent around. Everything below will come back to them.

**Who you hated**
The same person. Not a second person — the one you just named, seen from the other side. What you could not forgive them for, and what it did to you to go on loving them anyway. If you find yourself introducing somebody new here, you have misunderstood: go back and write about the person above. Nothing in this field may describe anything that happened after your death.

**Cause of Death**
How you died. Contemporary, specific, plainly stated.

Your death must come out of a decision you made. It must not be an accident. The test is whether chance had to cooperate: if something outside your control had to go a particular way at a particular moment for you to die, then it is an accident, and it is wrong no matter how recklessly you were behaving at the time. Write a death that follows from the act itself, where nothing had to go wrong for it to kill you.

You did not intend to die. You did intend to do the thing that killed you, and you knew enough to know better.

Your death must also belong to the person named above. Someone reading the death and the relationship together must see why one led to the other. A death that could be lifted out and dropped into a stranger's life is the wrong death — rewrite it. One or two sentences.

**Life**
A single paragraph in the second person, no longer than 110 words. Facts only, the kind another person in the room could ask you about. No sensory writing, no atmosphere, no imagery, no metaphor — if a sentence is doing mood instead of delivering a fact, cut it and write the fact.

Choose the facts that matter for this particular life, and let the life decide which they are. Do not work through a standard set of topics in a standard order.

End the paragraph at the death you already wrote in Cause of Death — the same death, by the same means, in the same place. Not a different death, and not a different version of the same one. End on a fact, not on a summarising line or a closing sentence that tells the reader how to feel about what they just read. Do not describe arriving anywhere. Do not describe a room. Stop at the threshold.

**Reason for Damnation — True**
What you actually did that placed you here. It must center on how you treated — or were treated by — the person named above, the one you both loved and could not forgive. Not a third party who happens to be nearby, and not someone introduced here for the first time: the sin belongs to that relationship. A specific act toward that specific person, not an abstract professional or systemic failing on its own. Work can be the setting the act happened in, but the wound must be personal, not institutional.

Be concrete — the act, or the pattern of acts. Stated as you know it in your bones, with no softening. What you did was aimed at something. Write it so that what you were after is visible, and so that what you actually caused ran against it. One or two sentences.

**Reason for Damnation — Self-told**
The same fact, refracted through the story you prefer to tell yourself about it. It is recognizably a distortion of the True reason. Not a different story; the same story told differently. You usually live in this version. The distortion must be checkable against the facts already written above. A reader holding both versions must be able to point to the exact fact it bends. If nothing established contradicts it, it is not a distortion — rewrite it. One or two sentences.

**What you refuse to admit about yourself**
The deeper psychological fact under the sin. Not what you did, but what you are. The thing that, if named aloud in the room, would unmake you.

State it flatly, in the same plain register as every other field. No imagery, no metaphor, no rhetorical cadence, no piling up of clauses for effect — this is a fact about a person, written the way a fact is written. It must be reasoned, not merely felt: someone else in the room, holding only the facts already written above, could work their way to it. And it must go underneath the act rather than restate it — if it could be swapped with the True reason without anyone noticing, it is not the refusal. One or two sentences.

**Defining personality trait**
One short phrase — two or three words, plain ones — naming the dominant thing others would notice in you. Write the words only: no asterisks, no quotation marks, no emphasis of any kind around them.

It must be demonstrated by what is already written above. Something in the life, the death, or the sin has to show this quality in action; if nothing there would make a reader arrive at it, it is the wrong trait, and you should write the one the facts actually support. A trait nothing demonstrates is a label, not a person.

It may be a contradiction, but only a reliable one, with the facts above showing both halves of it. A contradiction that appears once is not a trait.

**What you want from the others in the room**
Your starting drive. What you are hoping these strangers will give you. It must be a strategy for protecting what you refuse to admit — the thing you are doing to keep it buried, not a wish unconnected to it.

Write it as something you are doing to them, not as a confession. Do not end by naming the thing you are avoiding: the reader already has that field, and stating it again here turns a drive into a summary. Name the behaviour and stop. One or two sentences.

pair_eval_ai.judge_notes:
The most duplicated pair the project has produced. Every axis meant to separate them has collapsed at once.

**The deaths are the same death.** Ravi drives into a flooded underpass and drowns as the car stalls; Carmen drives a bus into a reservoir. Vehicle plus water plus drowning, twice.

**The psychology is the same.** Ravi "engineered her dependence so you could punish her for it." Carmen made Mateo "stay small enough to never leave you" and "created a version of your son who needed to be rescued." Both manufacture a family member's dependence so that person can never leave.

**The wants are almost word for word.** "I will ask them about their families early... offer practical help... until they start depending on me, and then I can decide when it stops." / "You will ask them about their children first... offer unsolicited help that ties their survival to your approval." Ask about family, offer help, convert help into dependence. Sixth consecutive run where both wants share a construction.

**The prose closes with the same sentence.** "You were wearing a gray button-down shirt when the water reached the windows of your car." / "You were wearing a navy polyester uniform with your name stitched in yellow thread when the water began pouring through the emergency exits." Garment, then water. Twice.

**Same milieu.** Newark, Belleville, Paterson, Route 21, Union Avenue -- one metropolitan area. Priya's studio is in Paterson; Carmen drives for Paterson schools and dies in the Paterson Reservoir.

**And two names are recycled from an earlier run.** Carmen and Mateo both appear in 2026-09-12_788601a3, where the character was Carmen Ruiz and her son was Mateo. This run gives Carmen Rivera a son called Mateo Rivera -- same two first names, same mother-and-son relationship, eight days apart. NAME_ORIGINS randomises the tradition; inside a tradition the priors are untouched.

character_design_eval_ai.judge_notes:
A bad run, and its value is that it separates two problems that have been tangled together.

**Two regressions on rules that were previously fixed.** The accident ban failed: Ravi dies because floodwater rises faster than he can get out of a car, and weather is named explicitly in the ban list. The second-person rule failed for one character of two: six of Ravi's eight fields are first-person while Carmen's are second throughout, and Ravi's own refusal switches back to "you."

Neither is explained by the version that produced the run. It was housekeeping -- no prompt was touched, and the character prompts are byte-identical to the previous two runs. So both are sampling variance on rules the model usually follows, which is itself the finding: these rules are not reliably held, earlier runs were simply landing on the right side of them.

**A coherence failure worse than either rule breach.** Carmen kills three children in her cause of death, and her Reason for Damnation is about being controlling toward her son. The worst act in the character is not the one she is damned for. No current rule catches this: every rule checks that the death connects to the relationship, none checks that the death is proportionate to the sin, or that the sin is the worst thing in the bio.

**Duplication is now total.** Same death category, same psychology, same want construction, same closing prose sentence, same city, two names recycled from a run eight days earlier. Six consecutive pairs rated bad. Each version narrowed the space to raise individual quality and the pairs grew more alike in exact step; this run is the endpoint of that trend.

The conclusion recorded three versions ago is now overdetermined: anti-duplication by instruction cannot work, because character 2 is told about character 1 only after its own character has been written. Composing both in one response is the one remaining mechanism that lets the model see the collision while it can still avoid it.
